submissions.findingTextShort: A 2024 six-study meta-analysis found no significant overall effect of ursolic acid on eleven cardiometabolic risk-factor outcomes.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis including six human intervention articles found that ursolic-acid supplementation, across reported doses of about 50.94 to 450 mg/day, did not significantly change body weight, BMI, waist circumference, body-fat percentage, lean body mass, systolic or diastolic blood pressure, fasting glucose, insulin, triglycerides, or HDL cholesterol compared with controls. This pooled null should constrain broad weight-loss, metabolic, and cardiometabolic benefit claims even though individual small studies have reported favorable signals.
submissions.populationContext: Adults represented across six intervention articles included in a systematic review/meta-analysis through February 2023.
submissions.usageContext: Ursolic-acid supplementation across approximately 50.94 to 450 mg/day in the included interventions.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Only six articles were available, interventions and populations varied, and a pooled null does not prove absence of every proposition-specific effect. It should, however, outrank generic mechanism-derived benefit language.

submissions.findingTextShort: A very small 12-week metabolic-syndrome RCT reported favorable weight, waist, fasting-glucose, and insulin-sensitivity changes with 150 mg/day ursolic acid.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: In a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled pilot trial, 24 untreated adults with metabolic syndrome received 150 mg/day ursolic acid or placebo for 12 weeks. The ursolic-acid group showed reported improvements in body weight, BMI, waist circumference, fasting glucose, insulin sensitivity, and a higher rate of transient metabolic-syndrome remission, while lipid profile, blood pressure, IL-6, and CRP did not significantly change. All 24 participants completed the trial and reported adverse events were mild and similar between groups.
submissions.populationContext: Twenty-four untreated adults aged 30 to 60 years with metabolic syndrome; 12 per group.
submissions.usageContext: Oral ursolic acid 150 mg once daily for 12 weeks versus homologated placebo.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: The sample was extremely small and several reported improvements were within-group comparisons. This signal must remain subordinate to the later pooled null and should not be marketed as established weight-loss or metabolic-syndrome treatment efficacy.

submissions.findingTextShort: An eight-week randomized trial found no added muscle-mass or strength benefit from 400 mg/day ursolic acid during resistance training and a high-protein diet.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: In a double-blind placebo-controlled trial of physically active young men undergoing resistance training while consuming a high-protein diet, 400 mg/day ursolic acid for eight weeks did not provide a significant additional benefit for muscle strength or muscle mass compared with placebo. The trial directly contradicts generic anabolic or hypertrophy claims extrapolated from preclinical pathways.
submissions.populationContext: Physically active young men undergoing resistance training; 22 participants were represented in the treatment and control groups reported in the trial.
submissions.usageContext: Ursolic acid 400 mg/day for eight weeks alongside resistance training and a high-protein diet.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Small sample and a specific trained/high-protein context limit generalization, but the direct null is first-class evidence against a guaranteed synergistic muscle-building effect.
